topics.legal_basis:
Mehr in Pakistan is legally recognized under Section 10 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance (MFLO), 1961. A wife can demand her mehr at any point during the marriage, and the husband is legally obligated to pay it.
Mehr is recorded in the Nikahnama at the time of marriage, and courts recognize a wife's right to it even where the Nikahnama is incomplete. Mehr belongs entirely to the wife as her personal property and can be claimed even after divorce.
topics.islamic_basis:
Surah An-Nisa
Quran
4:4
Verified
وَءَاتُوا۟ ٱلنِّسَآءَ صَدُقَـٰتِهِنَّ نِحْلَةً ۚ فَإِن طِبْنَ لَكُمْ عَن شَىْءٍ مِّنْهُ نَفْسًا فَكُلُوهُ هَنِيٓـًٔا مَّرِيٓـًٔا
And give the women [upon marriage] their [bridal] gifts graciously. But if they give up willingly to you anything of it, then take it in satisfaction and ease.
Brief Tafsir: This verse establishes mehr as an unconditional gift to the wife, prohibiting her guardians from taking it. The wife alone decides if she wishes to waive any portion.
View on Quran.com
verse 4,instructs husbands to give women their mehr willingly, as an obligation. In his commentary Tafheem-ul-Quran, Maulana Abul Ala Maududi explains this verse as establishing mehr as a duty owed directly to the wife, not to her guardians or family — a correction of a pre-Islamic practice where a woman's guardians would take her bridal-due for themselves. The verse also afﬁrms that a wife may, entirely of her own free will, choose to give up part of her mehr — meaning the choice belongs to her alone, not to her husband or family.

qa.question: Mera mehr ada nahi hua, kya main abhi bhi le sakti hoon?
qa.answer: Haan. Mehr aapka qanooni haq hai jo Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 ke tehat protect hai. Aap shaadi ke doran ya baad mein bhi mehr ka mutalba kar sakti hain, chahe talaq ho chuki ho. Behtar hoga ke apne Nikahnama ki copy nikalwayein aur zaroorat parne par Union Council ya family lawyer se raabta karein.if the husband dies before consummation, the full mehr is still due to the wife (Hanafi view), unless she agrees otherwise

qa.question: Kya sasural wale mera mehr rok saktay hain?
qa.answer: Nahin. Mehr sirf aapki milkiyat hai — na shohar, na sasural wale isay rok saktay hain. Quran mein Surah An-Nisa ki ayat 4 mein saaf kaha gaya hai ke mehr seedha biwi ko diya jaye, na ke uske sarparaston ko. Yeh aapka qanooni aur deeni dono lehaz se haq hai.

qa.question: Nikahnama mein mehr ki raqam likhi nahi gayi, kya phir bhi haq hai?
qa.answer: Haan, mehr ka haq khatam nahi hota chahe Nikahnama mein raqam waazeh na likhi ho. Aap apne family lawyer ya Union Council se rehnumai le sakti hain ke is soorat mein mehr ka tayin kaise hoga.

qa.question: Kya mein apna mehr maaf kar sakti hoon?
qa.answer: Haan, lekin yeh sirf aapki apni marzi se hona chahiye, kisi dabao ya majboori mein nahi. Quran isay khud biwi ka ikhtiyar batata hai — koi aur yeh faisla aapki taraf se nahi kar sakta.

qa.question: Talaq ke baad mehr ka kya hota hai?
qa.answer: Mehr talaq se khatam nahi hota. Agar mehr pehle se ada nahi hua tha, to talaq ke baad bhi aap iska mutalba kar sakti hain.

qa.question: Kya mehr sirf paison ki shakal mein hota hai?
qa.answer: Nahin, mehr paisa, zewar, jaidad ya koi bhi qeemti cheez ho sakti hai jo Nikah ke waqt tay ki gayi ho. Jo bhi tay hua ho, woh aapka haq hai.

topics.legal_basis: Maintenance rights are covered under Section 9 of the MFLO 1961. A husband is legally responsible for ﬁnancially maintaining his wife and children. If he fails to provide maintenance, the wife can approach the Union Council/Chairman, which can refer the matter to an Arbitration Council to enforce payment. If the Union Council's decision isn't satisfactory, there is a further right of revision before the Collector.

Surah An-Nisa, 
Quran
4:34
Verified
ٱلرِّجَالُ قَوَّٰمُونَ عَلَى ٱلنِّسَآءِ بِمَا فَضَّلَ ٱللَّهُ بَعْضَهُمْ عَلَىٰ بَعْضٍ وَبِمَآ أَنفَقُوا۟ مِنْ أَمْوَٰلِهِمْ ۚ فَٱلصَّـٰلِحَـٰتُ قَـٰنِتَـٰتٌ حَـٰفِظَـٰتٌ لِّلْغَيْبِ بِمَا حَفِظَ ٱللَّهُ ۚ وَٱلَّـٰتِى تَخَافُونَ نُشُوزَهُنَّ فَعِظُوهُنَّ وَٱهْجُرُوهُنَّ فِى ٱلْمَضَاجِعِ وَٱضْرِبُوهُنَّ ۖ فَإِنْ أَطَعْنَكُمْ فَلَا تَبْغُوا۟ عَلَيْهِنَّ سَبِيلًا ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ عَلِيًّا كَبِيرًا
Men are in charge of women by [right of] what Allāh has given one over the other and what they spend [for maintenance] from their wealth. So righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in [the husband's] absence what Allāh would have them guard. But those [wives] from whom you fear arrogance - [first] advise them; [then if they persist], forsake them in bed; and [finally], strike them [lightly]. But if they obey you [once more], seek no means against them. Indeed, Allāh is ever Exalted and Grand.
Brief Tafsir: The husband's financial responsibility is the basis of his qawwamah; it is a duty of care, not a right to control.
View on Quran.com
verse 34, describes men as qawwamun — a term Maulana Maududi's Tafheem-ul-Quran explains as someone responsible for the right conduct, safeguard, and maintenance of the affairs of the family, tied speciﬁcally to the fact that men spend of their wealth to support their wives. This ﬁnancial responsibility is the basis of the guardian role, not a license for control. Dr. Israr Ahmed, in his lecture on this topic, similarly clariﬁes that while men are designated as ﬁnancially responsible guardians, this role does not grant permission to neglect or oppress a wife's rights — the responsibility exists precisely to protect and provide for her, and misusing this authority to commit injustice is explicitly warned against.

qa.question: Mera shohar mujhe kharcha nahi deta, mein kya karoon?
qa.answer: Nafaqa (kharcha) dena shohar ki qanooni zimmedari hai, jo Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 ke Section 9 mein darj hai. Agar shohar ada nahi kar raha, aap apne ilaqe ke Union Council mein darkhwast de sakti hain, jahan Arbitration Council maamla dekhegi. Agar wahan se insaaf na mile, aap Collector ke paas revision ke liye ja sakti hain.

qa.question: Kya talaq ke baad bhi nafaqa mil sakta hai?
qa.answer: Iddat ke doran nafaqa ka haq mojood hota hai. Har case mukhtalif ho sakta hai, is liye apne mahol ke mutabiq kisi family lawyer ya Union Council se mashwara zaroor karein.

qa.question: Islam mein shohar par kharche ki zimmedari kyun hai?
qa.answer: Quran, Surah An-Nisa ayat 34 mein, mardon ko "qawwam" kaha gaya hai — yani woh jo apne maal se apni family ka kharcha uthata hai aur unki hifazat karta hai. Yeh zimmedari aurat ko dabane ke liye nahi, balke uski dekhbhal aur tahafuz ke liye di gayi hai.

qa.question: Agar shohar kaam nahi karta ya kharcha dene se inkaar kare, to kya yeh Islami taleemat ke khilaf hai?
qa.answer: Haan, nafaqa dena shohar par farz hai. Agar woh jaan boojh kar apni zimmedari se inkaar kare, yeh uski deeni zimmedari se hatna hai. Aap qanooni raasta (Union Council, Arbitration Council) istemal kar sakti hain apna haq lene ke liye.

qa.question: Kya sirf khana aur kapda hi nafaqa hai, ya aur bhi cheezein shamil hain?
qa.answer: Nafaqa mein rehaish, khana, kapda, aur zaroori zindagi ke kharche shamil hain. Yeh mahol aur waqt ke mutabiq tay hota hai — jo us ilaqe mein munasib samjha jaye.

qa.question: Kya sasural walon ka kharcha bhi shohar par farz hai, ya sirf biwi ka?
qa.answer: Shohar ki bunyadi zimmedari apni biwi aur bachon ka kharcha uthana hai. Sasural walon ka kharcha alag maamla hai aur is par qanooni rai family lawyer se lena behtar hoga.

topics.islamic_basis: Surah An-Nisa, verse 29, instructs believers not to consume one another's wealth through falsehood or deception, and only through mutually agreed, lawful transactions. This principle — that wealth must never be taken from someone through trickery, pressure, or dishonesty — is the Quranic foundation for why scams, fraud, and exploitation of the vulnerable are considered a serious wrong, not just a legal offense.

qa.question: Mujhe kisi ne call kiya aur bola woh bank se hai, mera ATM PIN maanga, kya karoon?
qa.answer: Kabhi bhi apna ATM PIN, OTP ya password kisi ko na batayein, chahe woh khud ko bank ka numainda kahe. Asli banks kabhi phone par yeh maloomat nahi maangte. Agar shak ho, foran apne bank ko khud call karein (jo number aapke pass pehle se ho) aur is waqia ki report NCCIA helpline 1991 par karein.

qa.question: Agar mere account se paise ghalat tareeqe se nikal gaye hain, kya wapas mil saktay hain?
qa.answer: Haan, agar transfer aapki ijazat ke baghair hua hai, State Bank ke qawaid ke mutabiq bank ki zimmedari hai ke woh saabit kare ke transfer aapki marzi se hua. Foran apne bank ko inform karein, aur agar bank sahi jawab na de to Banking Mohtasib Pakistan (0800-44522) par mufta shikayat darj karwayein.

qa.question: Koi mujhe bol raha hai ke thora paisa lagayen aur double mil jayega, kya karoon?
qa.answer: Yeh aksar dhoka hota hai. Koi bhi asli sarmaya kaari (investment) itni jaldi double munafa nahi deti. Aisi offers se bachein, aur kisi bhi paisa lagane se pehle kisi bharosemand bank ya family member se mashwara zaroor karein.

qa.question: Mujhe naya SIM lene gayi thi, dukandar ne mera angootha lagaya aur bola SIM kal milega, kya yeh theek hai?
qa.answer:
Yeh ek jaana pehchana dhoka hai jahan aapke angoothe ke nishan ka ghalat istemal karke
doosra SIM activate kiya ja sakta hai. Sirf ofﬁcially registered franchise se hi SIM lein, aur agar shak ho to PTA ko report karein.

qa.question: Mujhe WhatsApp par job ka offer mila hai jisme pehle paisa jama karwana keh rahe hain, kya yeh sahi hai?
qa.answer: Nahin, asli companies kabhi job dene se pehle paisa nahi maangti. Yeh ek aam scam hai. Aise kisi bhi offer mein paisa na bhejein aur agar shak ho to NCCIA helpline 1991 par report karein.

qa.question: Kisi ne mujhe mera CNIC number aur tasveer maang li, kya yeh dena chahiye?
qa.answer: Sirf unhi jagah apni CNIC details dein jo aap achi tarah jaanti hon aur bharosemand hon (jaise bank, sarkari daftar). Anjaan logon, calls, ya online forms ko apni CNIC details na dein — is se identity theft ho sakti hai.

topics.legal_basis: Nisab is the minimum amount of wealth a Muslim must own before Zakat becomes obligatory. Think of it as a "starting line" — if your qualifying wealth is below this line, you owe no Zakat at all. If you're at or above it, Zakat becomes due on the whole qualifying amount.

qa.question: What is Nisab?
qa.answer: Nisab is the minimum amount of wealth a Muslim must own before Zakat becomes obligatory. Think of it as a "starting line" — if your qualifying wealth is below this line, you owe no Zakat at all. If you're at or above it, Zakat becomes due on the whole qualifying amount.

topics.legal_basis:
## **The One Lunar Year Rule (Hawl)**

For cash, gold, silver, business stock, and livestock, your wealth must stay at or above Nisab for one full Islamic (lunar) year — 354 days — before Zakat is due on it.

_Hadith: Narrated Ali ibn AbuTalib: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you possess two hundred dirhams and one year passes on them, five dirhams are payable. Nothing is incumbent on you, that is, on gold, till it reaches twenty dinars. When you possess twenty dinars and one year passes on them, half a dinar is payable. Whatever exceeds, that will be reckoned properly."_

_—_ [_Sunan Abi Dawud 1573_](https://themuslimgpt.com/hadith/abudawud/1573) _· Sahih_

## **Your Zakat Anniversary Date**

Pick one fixed date each year (e.g., 1st of Ramadan) as your personal "Zakat day." On that date, calculate 2.5% of everything you currently hold that qualifies — it doesn't matter when during the year you earned each portion.

The hadith from Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) explicitly states:

_It was narrated that:Aishah said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah(ﷺ) say: 'There is not Zakat on wealth until Hawl (one year) has passed.' "_

_—_ [_Sunan Ibn Majah 1792_](https://themuslimgpt.com/hadith/ibnmajah/1792) _· Sahih_

## **Immediate Payment (Harvest & Minerals)**

- Crops: No waiting year needed — Zakat is paid right at harvest, even if you harvest more than once a year.
- Minerals & buried treasure: Paid immediately at the moment of discovery.

topics.legal_basis:
## **Category 1: Gold, Silver & Cash**

This is the most common category — your savings, cash on hand, gold, and silver.

Hadith:The Prophet ﷺ said:

_Narrated Abu Saʿid:Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said, "No Zakat is due on property mounting to less than five Uqiyas (of silver), and no Zakat is due on less than five camels, and there is no Zakat on less than five Wasqs." (A Wasqs equals 60 Sa's) & (1 Sa=3 K gms App)_

_—_ [_Sahih al-Bukhari 1405_](https://themuslimgpt.com/hadith/bukhari/1405) _· Sahih_

| **Detail** | **Value**                                                                             |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Nisab      | 85g of 24K gold (~97.1g for 21K gold), OR 595g of silver, OR cash equal to that value |
| Rate       | 2.5% paid once a year on your Zakat anniversary date                                  |

## **Category 2: Trade Goods & Business Assets**

If you run a business, Zakat applies to everything you hold for sale — inventory, raw materials, finished products, and business cash.

| **Detail** | **Value**                                                                    |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Nisab      | Market value equal to 85g gold or 595g silver                                |
| Rate       | 2.5% yearly on the total wholesale value of sellable stock and business cash |

## **Category 3: Agricultural Produce (Ushr)**

Zakat on farm produce is called Ushr. Unlike cash, there's no one-year wait — it's paid the day you harvest.

Hadith:

_Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:No Sadaqa (zakat) is due on less than five wasqs of (dates or grains), on less than five camel-heads, and on less than five uqiyas (of silver)_

_—_ [_Sahih Muslim 2266_](https://themuslimgpt.com/hadith/muslim/2266) _· Sahih_

| **Detail**                    | **Value**                                           |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Nisab                         | 5 Wasqs (~653 kg / 1,440 lbs of dry grain or fruit) |
| Rate (rain/river fed)         | 10% — no irrigation cost was paid                   |
| Rate (artificially irrigated) | 5% — water was pumped/paid for                      |
| Timing                        | Paid immediately at harvest                         |

## **Category 4: Livestock**

Applies to free-grazing animals raised for their produce (milk, breeding), not for resale.

| **Detail** | **Value**                                                  |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Nisab      | Minimum 5 camels, 30 cows/buffaloes, or 40 sheep/goats     |
| Rate       | Fixed numbers of animals owed, based on herd-size brackets |

_Note: Livestock raised to be sold commercially is treated as a business trade asset (2.5% rule), not under the livestock rules._

## **Category 5: Minerals & Buried Treasure (Rikaz)**

Covers valuable resources extracted from the earth, or ancient treasure found with no known owner.

| **Detail** | **Value**                                                              |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Nisab      | None — applies to any significant find                                 |
| Rate       | 20% (1/5th, called Khumus), paid immediately upon extraction/discovery |

topics.legal_basis:
The Qur'an (Surah at-Tawbah, 9:60) names exactly eight groups who may receive Zakat funds:

- Al-Fuqara' (The Poor) — people with severe poverty and virtually no income or assets.
- Al-Masakin (The Needy) — people who earn something, but it's not enough to cover basic needs.
- Al-'Amilina 'Alayha (Zakat Administrators) — officials appointed to collect and distribute Zakat.
- Al-Mu'allafatu Qulubuhum (Reconciled Hearts) — new converts or people being welcomed into the Muslim community.
- Fi al-Riqab (Freeing Captives) — people working to free themselves from slavery or bondage.
- Al-Gharimin (The Debt-Ridden) — people with legitimate survival debts they can't repay.
- Fi Sabilillah (In the Cause of Allah) — those striving in religious education, community welfare, or defense.
- Ibn al-Sabil (The Stranded Traveler) — travelers cut off from their money who need help getting home.

- Al-'Amilina 'Alayha (Zakat Administrators) — officials appointed to collect and distribute Zakat.
- Al-Mu'allafatu Qulubuhum (Reconciled Hearts) — new converts or people being welcomed into the Muslim community.
- Fi al-Riqab (Freeing Captives) — people working to free themselves from slavery or bondage.
- Al-Gharimin (The Debt-Ridden) — people with legitimate survival debts they can't repay.
- Fi Sabilillah (In the Cause of Allah) — those striving in religious education, community welfare, or defense.
- Ibn al-Sabil (The Stranded Traveler) — travelers cut off from their money who need help getting home.

topics.legal_basis:
Everything above is Zakat al-Mal (wealth Zakat). Zakat al-Fitr is different — smaller, simpler, and tied to Ramadan, not to yearly wealth.

- Who pays: Every Muslim, regardless of Nisab — a head of household pays on behalf of dependents too.
- When: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, at the end of Ramadan.
- Amount: About one Sa' (roughly 2.5–3 kg) of a staple food, or its cash equivalent.
- Purpose: Purifies the fasting person's Ramadan and ensures the poor can also celebrate Eid.
- Hadith:

_Narrated ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar:The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered (Muslims) to give one Sa' of dates or one Sa' of barley as Zakat-ul-Fitr. The people regarded two Mudds of wheat as equal to that_

_—_ [_Sahih al-Bukhari 1507_](https://themuslimgpt.com/hadith/bukhari/1507) _· Sahih_

topics.legal_basis:
Zakat rules were established for a simpler economy — cash, gold, livestock, crops. Today's financial world has salaries, stock markets, pension accounts, and rental properties that don't map onto the old categories perfectly. Scholars generally agree on the underlying principles, but differ on how exactly to apply them to these newer forms of wealth. Below is a closer look at the most common cases, each with a simple worked example.

## **Salary & Employment Income**

A monthly salary isn't a traditional Zakat category on its own — it's simply cash once it lands in your account. Most contemporary scholars therefore treat it exactly like the cash you already save: it gets added to your total savings, and the one-year Hawl rule applies to the combined amount, calculated from your fixed Zakat anniversary date.

The debated part is timing: some scholars allow paying Zakat on each salary payment separately, as soon as it's received (a "pay-as-you-earn" approach), instead of waiting for the annual date. Both approaches are considered valid; the annual method is more common and simpler to track.

_Note: Example: Your Zakat anniversary is 1st Ramadan. Throughout the year your salary adds up in your bank account alongside existing savings. On 1st Ramadan, you total everything in the account — salary residue plus prior savings — and pay 2.5% on that combined figure, provided it's above Nisab._

## **Stocks & Shares**

Zakat treatment depends on why you're holding the shares:

- Active trading (buying and selling for short-term profit): treated like trade goods. Zakat is due on the full current market value of your holdings at 2.5%.
- Long-term investment (holding for dividends/growth, not reselling): many scholars say you only owe Zakat on the company's underlying zakatable assets (cash, inventory) proportional to your shareholding — not the full share price, since much of a company's value sits in non-zakatable assets like factories or equipment. In practice, this is hard to calculate precisely, so some scholars simplify it to roughly 25–30% of the share's market value, or zakat only on dividends received.

_Note: Example: You hold \$10,000 worth of shares purely for long-term growth, and don't plan to sell them soon. Using the simplified approach, you might pay 2.5% on an estimated ~~30% of that value (~~\$3,000), i.e. around \$75, rather than 2.5% on the full \$10,000. A trader holding the same \$10,000 for quick resale would instead pay 2.5% on the full amount (~\$250)._

## **Retirement & Pension Funds**

The key question is accessibility — can you withdraw the money now, or is it locked away until retirement?

- Inaccessible funds (e.g., an employer pension you can't touch until retirement age): most scholars say no Zakat is due yet, since you don't truly own or control the wealth. Zakat becomes due once you actually receive it — some say for that year only, others say backdated for the years it accumulated, depending on the scholar.
- Accessible funds (e.g., a personal investment account you could withdraw from anytime, even with a penalty): more likely to be zakatable annually like ordinary savings, since you have real access to it.

_Note: Example: You have \$50,000 in a workplace pension you cannot withdraw until age 60. No Zakat is due on it yearly. When you retire and receive the funds, you'd then start applying Zakat to it going forward, similar to any other cash you hold._

## **Real Estate**

The rule depends entirely on the property's purpose:

- Your own home: never zakatable, regardless of its value — it's a personal-use asset, not wealth held for growth.
- Rental property you intend to keep long-term: the property itself isn't zakatable, but the rental income you collect is treated as cash and included in your annual Zakat calculation (after deducting expenses/debts).
- Property bought purely to resell for profit: treated as a trade good, so the full current market value is zakatable at 2.5% every year it remains unsold.

_Note: Example: You own an apartment you rent out for \$1,000/month and keep no intention to sell it. Over the year you collect \$12,000 in rent; after normal expenses, whatever remains in savings on your Zakat date is combined with your other cash and zakated at 2.5%. The apartment's own market value is not zakated. If instead you'd bought that same apartment purely to flip and sell, its full market value would be zakated annually at 2.5% until sold._

topics.title_en: 11. Does Zakat Apply to Both Men and Women?
topics.legal_basis:
Yes — Zakat applies equally to both women and men. It is not tied to gender at all; it is tied purely to wealth ownership.

## **Ownership Is the Only Condition**

Any Muslim adult — male or female — who personally owns wealth at or above Nisab for a full lunar year owes Zakat on it, calculated and paid the exact same way (2.5% on cash, gold, silver, business assets, and so on).

## **A Woman's Wealth Is Entirely Her Own**

In Islamic law, a wife's income, savings, gold, property, or business assets belong solely to her — they are not automatically merged with her husband's wealth. If she owns qualifying wealth, she is personally responsible for her own Zakat, separate from her husband's.

## **Gold Jewelry: The One Debated Area**

This is the main point of scholarly difference, and it applies mostly to women since they are the more common holders of jewelry:

- Hanafi school: personal-use gold/silver jewelry is zakatable if it reaches Nisab, no matter how "customary" the amount is.
- Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali schools: jewelry worn regularly for personal use is generally exempt, as long as it stays within reasonable, customary limits and isn't hoarded as an investment.

## **Spouses Are Independently Responsible**

A husband is not obligated to pay Zakat on his wife's wealth, and a wife is not obligated to pay on her husband's — each person's obligation is based only on what they individually own. A husband may choose to pay it on her behalf if she asks and he agrees, but the responsibility itself remains legally hers.

Before going into detail, here are the core terms used throughout this guide, each explained in one or two plain sentences. Every term is unpacked more fully in its own section below — use this list as a quick lookup, not a replacement for the full explanation.

| Term                       | Simple Definition                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Hiba**                   | A gift. Something you give away to someone else while you're still alive — once it's handed over, it's completely theirs.                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Wasiyyah**               | An Islamic will. Instructions for what happens to _part_ of your property after you die — limited to at most one-third of your estate.                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Waqf**                   | A permanent charitable endowment. You lock up an asset (like land or a building) forever for a good cause — it can never be sold, given away, or inherited again; only its benefit (like rent, crops, or use) keeps flowing to people.                                                                                       |
| **Sadaqah Jariyah**        | "Ongoing charity" — any voluntary good deed that keeps benefiting people (and earning you reward) even after you've stopped actively giving. A Waqf is one specific, formal type of Sadaqah Jariyah; the term itself is broader and includes simpler things too, like sharing a benefit that keeps helping others over time. |
| **Halal Investing**        | Putting your money into the stock market or other investments in a way that avoids interest (riba) and avoids companies involved in forbidden activities (alcohol, gambling, conventional banking, etc.).                                                                                                                    |
| **Takaful**                | The Islamic alternative to insurance. Instead of paying a company a "premium" to take on your risk, you and other participants pool money together as donations, and the pool pays out to whoever in the group suffers a loss.                                                                                               |
| **Tabarru'**               | The donation-style contribution a Takaful participant pays into the shared pool. Calling it a "donation" rather than a "premium" is what keeps the arrangement Shariah-compliant, since it's cooperative giving, not a commercial bet.                                                                                       |
| **Wakala Waqf Model**      | The specific structure most Takaful companies in Pakistan use: the operator manages the pool for a fee (_wakala_ = agency), and part of the contributions sits inside a dedicated waqf fund that exists just to pay claims and hold surplus.                                                                                 |
| **Nisab**                  | The minimum amount of wealth a person must have before an obligation like Zakat applies to them. (Referenced here for contrast — Waqf and Sadaqah Jariyah have no Nisab; see Section 3.)                                                                                                                                     |
| **Custody (Hizanat)**      | The right and responsibility to raise a child day-to-day — feeding, nursing, physical care, and upbringing.                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Guardianship (Wilayat)** | The legal authority to make binding decisions and sign contracts on a minor's behalf — including selling or managing property that legally belongs to the child. Separate from custody (see above).                                                                                                                          |
| **Property Guardian**      | A person formally appointed by a court specifically to manage and, if necessary, sell a minor's property — a mother with custody does not automatically have this power; it requires a separate court appointment.                                                                                                           |

topics.legal_basis:
**In plain words:** A Hiba is something you give away completely, right now, while you're alive. Once you hand it over and the other person accepts it, it's theirs — no take-backs, and it has nothing to do with the fixed inheritance shares that apply after death.

A Hiba is something given away while the giver is still alive — once it's properly handed over, it belongs completely to the receiver from that moment on.

**Hadith:**

The Prophet ﷺ said, as narrated by Zaid bin Thabit:

_"Whoever gives a life-long gift, it belongs to the one to whom he gave it, both during his life and after his death. And do not give things on the basis of Ruqba, for whoever is given something on the basis of Ruqba, it becomes part of his estate."_ — Sunan an-Nasa'i 3723, Sahih

Inheritance is completely different: it only takes effect after someone dies, and it follows fixed shares set by Islamic law, not personal choice.

**For a Hiba to count as valid, three things must happen:** 1. The giver declares the gift. 2. The receiver accepts it. 3. Actual possession is handed over.

A gift involves no monetary consideration — this distinguishes it from a sale or exchange. Once properly completed, a Hiba cannot be revoked, and the receiver cannot be forced to give anything back in exchange.

_Scenario: Fatima's father owns a small shop. While he's alive and in good health, he decides to gift the shop entirely to Fatima — he signs it over, hands her the keys, and she starts running it. This is a valid Hiba: the shop is now completely hers, and this gift does not reduce or replace whatever inheritance share she'll still be legally entitled to later, when her father passes away and the estate is divided among all his heirs._

### The Pakistan-Specific Problem to Know

This exact tool is sometimes misused. Research on Pakistani family law shows that **"Hiba Tafzili"** (preferential gifting) is often used as a tool to alienate women from their ancestral property, and Pakistani courts show inconsistent rulings on this practice — meaning some fathers gift away most or all property to sons while alive, specifically to leave daughters with little left to inherit later. Knowing the difference between a Hiba and inheritance helps a woman recognize when this is happening to her.

_Sources: Khaleej Times — "Islamic Inheritance: Hiba"; iPleaders — "Concept of Gift Under Islamic Law"; Al-Amir Law Journal (Pakistan) — research paper on Hiba Tafzili and women's inheritance rights._

**In plain words:** A Wasiyyah is different from a Hiba because it only kicks in after you die — and unlike a gift, you can't will away everything. You're only allowed to redirect up to one-third of your estate through a will; the rest automatically goes to your legal heirs in their fixed Quranic shares, no matter what the will says.

A Muslim may give away their entire property during their lifetime through a gift, but only one-third of the total estate can be bequeathed through a will. The remaining two-thirds must automatically follow the fixed Quranic inheritance shares — a will cannot override those shares or redirect that portion to someone who is already a legal heir.

**Hadith:**

The Prophet ﷺ said:

_"You may bequeath one-third, and one-third is a lot."_

It was narrated from 'Aishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to visit Sa'd (when he was sick). Sa'd said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I bequeath two-thirds of my wealth?" He said: "No." He said: "Shall I bequeath half?" He said: "No." He said: "Shall I bequeath one-third?" He said: _"Yes, one-third, and one-third is much or large. If you leave your heirs independent of means that is better than if you leave them poor, holding out their hands… It is not right for a Muslim who has anything to bequeath to spend two nights without having his will written down."_ — Sunan an-Nasa'i 3633, Sahih

_Scenario: Sara wants to leave something extra to a needy niece who wouldn't normally inherit under fixed Islamic shares (since a niece isn't a primary heir when Sara has children of her own). Sara can legally will up to one-third of her estate to that niece. But she cannot will away more than a third, and she cannot use the will to reduce her own daughter's guaranteed inheritance share or redirect it elsewhere — that portion is locked in by Islamic law regardless of what the will states._

_Sources: iPleaders — "Concept of Gift Under Islamic Law"; IslamWeb Fatwa Center — "Difference Between Will and Gift."_

**In plain words:** Sadaqah Jariyah just means "ongoing charity" — any good deed that keeps helping people and keeps earning you reward long after you've done it. A Waqf is a specific, formal way of doing this: you permanently lock up an asset (like land, a building, or money) for a charitable purpose. Zakat is obligatory and calculated precisely, with a fixed percentage and a minimum threshold (Nisab) that must be met before it applies. Waqf and Sadaqah Jariyah are different: they are entirely voluntary, with no fixed amount and no Nisab — the giver decides both the amount and the cause.

**Sadaqah Jariyah** ("ongoing charity") is the broader concept: any voluntary act of charity that keeps generating reward for the giver even after they've stopped actively giving, because the benefit keeps flowing to others indefinitely.

It can never be sold, inherited, or taken back; only its ongoing benefit or income continues to serve the cause. The Prophet ﷺ said:

**In plain words:** Avoiding interest (riba) doesn't mean avoiding the stock market entirely — it means being picky about _which_ companies you put money into. Pakistan has a built-in system that pre-screens companies for you, so you don't have to research each one yourself.

Avoiding interest doesn't mean avoiding the stock market altogether — it means being selective about which companies to invest in. In Pakistan, this has been made fairly accessible through a dedicated Shariah-screening system.

The **KMI-30 Index** tracks the 30 most liquid Shariah-compliant companies listed on the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX), weighted by market capitalization with a 12% cap on any single company's weight. Beyond just those 30, Islamic scholars — including those on Meezan Bank's Shariah Supervisory Board — along with SECP's own published Shariah screening guidelines from August 2022, have formally ruled that investing in Shariah-compliant equities on PSX is permissible, since it means becoming a part-owner of a real, operating business rather than gambling.

_Scenario: Hina has Rs. 100,000 in savings and wants to invest instead of leaving it idle, but she doesn't want to research individual stocks or risk accidentally investing in an interest-based bank or a company selling alcohol. Instead of picking stocks herself, she buys units of the KSE Meezan Index Fund, a Shariah-compliant fund designed to track the KMI-30 by investing in the same companies in proportion to their weight in the index. This way her investment automatically stays within Shariah-screened companies without her needing to verify each one manually._

_Sources: Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) — "Shariah Compliant Investment" page; Al Meezan Group — KSE Meezan Index Fund page; Hawksglobal.pk — "Halal Stocks Pakistan Guide" (2026)._

topics.legal_basis:
**In plain words:** Regular insurance is problematic in Islam mainly because of interest and too much uncertainty in how premiums and payouts work. Takaful fixes this by turning it into a group effort: everyone puts money into a shared pool as a _donation_, and whoever in the group has a loss gets paid out from that same pool — nobody is betting against anybody else.

Conventional insurance is considered problematic in Islam mainly because of interest and excessive uncertainty in how premiums and payouts work. Takaful solves this by turning it into a cooperative pool instead of a profit-driven contract. Participants pay contributions in the form of donations to help others in need, and instead of passing risk to an insurer, they share the risk together.

Each participant contributes to a common fund — the **takaful pool** — and the amount paid is treated as a donation (**tabarru'**), not a premium. In the **wakala waqf model**, part of the contribution goes to a separate waqf fund, which adds an extra layer of charity on top of the risk-sharing itself.

In Pakistan specifically, the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) has supported the industry's growth, and the **Takaful Rules of 2012** allowed conventional insurers to launch dedicated Takaful windows. The dominant structure used in Pakistan is the **"wakala waqf"** model.

_Scenario: Amina runs a small home-based business and wants to protect her equipment against fire or theft, but doesn't want to use a conventional insurance policy because of the interest and uncertainty involved. She takes a Takaful plan instead: she contributes a set amount into a shared pool with other participants. If her equipment is damaged, she's compensated from that pool. If no one in the pool makes a claim that year, any leftover surplus is either shared back among participants or reinvested for their benefit — unlike conventional insurance, where leftover surplus simply becomes company profit._

_Sources: SmartBenefits.pk — "Understanding Takaful: The Emerging Role of Islamic Insurance in Pakistan"; Habib Insurance — "How Takaful Works & Why You Should Consider It"; The Actuary (UK) — "Takaful Models of Islamic Insurance."_

topics.legal_basis:
**In plain words:** Raising a child day-to-day (custody) and having the legal authority to manage a child's money or property (guardianship) are two separate things in Pakistani law. A mother almost always gets the first one automatically. The second one — especially the power to sell or transfer a child's property — usually requires a separate court appointment, even for the mother.

This matters most for widowed or divorced women. In Pakistan, custody (day-to-day care) and guardianship (legal authority over decisions and property) are two separate things. Custody is the bringing up, nursing, and fostering of the child on a day-to-day basis, whereas guardianship means the power to carry out legal transactions and contracts with responsibility for the legal consequences.

Traditionally, the father is treated as the natural guardian, while the mother has priority for custody of boys until around age 7 and girls until puberty under Hanafi law, subject to the child's overall welfare. **The important financial detail:** a mother can be the de facto guardian of a minor's property, but she has no power to actually transfer or sell it. Alienating a minor's immovable property is only possible by the person legally entitled to be appointed property guardian, after obtaining the court's permission.

_Scenario: Sadia is widowed, and her late husband's life insurance payout and some property are meant for their two young children. She has automatic day-to-day custody and can raise them normally, but if she ever needs to sell an inherited plot of land that legally belongs to her children — say, to fund their education — she cannot do this on her own signature alone. Under the Guardian and Wards Act 1890, she would generally need to formally apply to the family court to be recognized as their legal property guardian before she can transact on their behalf. Knowing this in advance prevents delays or a transaction being challenged later as invalid._

_Sources: SAHSOL (Shaikh Ahmad Hassan School of Law, LUMS) — "Law on the Custody of Children in Pakistan"; CourtingTheLaw.com — "Law of Appointment of Guardian Under the Guardian & Wards Act 1890"; SJ Law Experts — "Guardianship Under Islamic Law in Pakistan."_

topics.legal_basis:
- **Mirath (Gross Inheritance):** All movable or immovable property left behind by the deceased, whether earned, inherited, or gifted. 

- **Warith (Heir):** A relative who may potentially inherit from the deceased's wealth. 

- **Wassiya (Will):** An order allocating a portion of the deceased's property, executed only after death. A will can only cover up to **1/3 of the estate** ; any excess is capped at 1/3. A will **cannot** be made in favor of a person who is already a legal heir (warith). 

- **Walad / Awlaad (Children, "CH"):** Son (S), daughter (D), son's son (SS), son's daughter (SD), son's son's son (SSS), son's son's daughter (SSD). Other grandchildren (e.g., daughter's children) are _not_ included in "CH" and fall under Dhil-Irham instead. 

- **Ikhwa (Siblings, "IK"):** Two or more real, paternal, or maternal brothers/sisters, regardless of type or gender. 

   - **Real brother/sister (RB/RS):** Same parents as deceased ( _haqiqi_ ). 

   - **Paternal brother/sister (PB/PS):** mother ( _allati_ ). 

   - **Maternal brother/sister (MT):** father ( _akhyafi_ ). 

- **Dhil-Furoodh:** ("sharers"). 

- **Asbah (Residuary, "Res"):** 

take whatever remains after Dhil-Furoodh are paid. Generally male relatives connected through a chain of males (exceptions: real sister and paternal sister can be residuaries in some configurations). 

- **Dhil-Irham (DI):** 3rd-tier heirs, entitled only if there is leftover property and no Asbah exists. The closest relative in this category takes everything remaining. 

- **Kalala:** A person who, at death, has no living children (S, D, SS, SD, SSS, SSD) and no living father or grandfather.

**Step 1:** Write the deceased's name, date of death, and distributable wealth (the amount remaining after steps 1–4 of wealth distribution above). 

**Step 2:** List all relatives alive at time of death. Mark any relative who qualifies for extended Residuary (Asbah) status with "R" (male relatives connected via a chain of males). 

**Step 3a:** Use Table 1 to assign shares to each applicable heir based on conditions. 

**Step 3b:** For these 5 relation-pairs, if both the male and female version are present, ignore the female's Table 1 share (mark with ") and extract her share from Table 2 instead: 

1. Son (S) & Daughter (D) 

2. Son's son (SS) & Son's daughter (SD) 

3. Son's son's son (SSS) & Son's son's daughter (SSD) 

4. Real brother (RB) & Real sister (RS) 

5. Paternal brother (PB) & Paternal sister (PS) 

**Step 4:** Find the LCM (lowest common multiple) of the denominators of assigned shares (can be skipped if using the "Share from 24" column directly — denominator is always 24 or less). Example: shares of 1/6, 1/2, 1/8 → LCM = 24 → numerators become 4, 12, 3 out of 24. 

**Step 5:** Calculate remaining shares = common denominator − sum of assigned numerators. Example: 24 − (4+12+3) = 5 remaining shares. 

**Step 6:** Move left→right through Table 2. Assign all remaining shares to the first applicable category. If that category is one of the 5 relation-pairs from Step 3b, males get 2x the share of females (multiply male count ×2, add female count, divide shares by that total, give 2 portions per male and 1 per female). 

- Example: 2 Sons + 2 Daughters assigned 12 shares → (2×2)+2 = 6 → 12/6 = 2 shares per unit → each son gets 4, each daughter gets 2. 

**Step 6b:** If shares are assigned to the extended Residuary (Asbah) category via Table 2, use **Table 3** to find the nearest qualifying Asbah relative. 

**Step 7:** Divide the shares in each category by the number of individuals in that category to get each person's portion. If division produces a decimal, multiply the entire column by the needed factor to keep whole numbers (e.g., 13 shares ÷ 6 people → multiply by 6 → 78 total shares, 13 each). 

**Step 8:** Convert shares into wealth terms using: 

**(Share of the person ÷ Total shares) × Total wealth = Wealth share of each person** 

**Two exceptions to watch for:** Problem of Excess ( _Masla-Radd_ ) and Problem of Deficiency ( _Masla-Aul_ ) — see Section 6 below.

1. **Homicide:** inheriting from them, even with a prescribed share. _"One who kills a man cannot inherit from him."_ (Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Abu Dawud) 

2. A non-Muslim cannot inherit from a Muslim, and vice versa. A will (up to 1/3) can be used to provide for a nonMuslim relative instead. _"A Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever, a disbeliever does not inherit from a Muslim."_ (Sahih Bukhari & Muslim, Book of Fara'id) 

3. **Illegitimate Child:** A child born out of wedlock is legally regarded only as the child of the mother. Falsely denying paternity is considered a major sin. (Reference: case of _Lian_ during the Prophet's lifetime, Sahih Bukhari, Book of Fara'id) 

_rules apply to individual cases._

topics.title_en: 11. Sources of Knowledge for Calculations (Quranic References)**
topics.legal_basis:
1. **Surah An-Nisa 4:11** (children & parents) — male share = 2× female share; 2+ daughters (no son) get 2/3; 1 daughter gets 1/2; each parent gets 1/6 if deceased left children; if no children, mother gets 1/3 (or 1/6 if deceased had siblings) — after bequests/debts. 

2. **Surah An-Nisa 4:12** (spouses) — husband gets 1/2 (no child) or 1/4 (with child); wife/wives get 1/4 (no child) or 1/8 (with child); siblings (kalala case) each get 1/6, or share 1/3 if more than two — after bequests/debts. 

3. **Surah An-Nisa 4:13–14** — these are Allah's set limits; obedience leads to Paradise, transgression to punishment. 

4. **Surah An-Nisa 4:176** — kalala ruling: a sole sister gets half of what brother left; two+ sisters get two-thirds; if both brothers and sisters, male gets share of two females. 

5. **Ibn Masud (RA)** narration — daughter gets 1/2, son's daughter gets 1/6 (together = 2/3), remainder to the sister. (Sahih Bukhari, Book of Fara'id)

a team can: (a) see the actual primary sources, (b) understand where Islamic jurisprudence and Pakistani statutory law agree/diverge, and (c) turn it into simplified, cited answers for end users. Every factual claim is footnoted to a real, checkable source; unconfirmed claims are flagged explicitly. 

**Scope/honesty note:** Not legal advice — for the document's authors, the AI agent's builders, or eventual end users. Pakistani family law is genuinely contested: statutes are amended provincially (family law devolved to provinces after the 18th Amendment), courts issue conflicting judgments reconciled over years, and religious interpretation differs by school of thought (Sunni Hanafi majority, Shia Ithna Ashari minority, others). This is a strong, sourced starting map — not a substitute for a licensed Pakistani family lawyer reviewing the agent's actual output before launch.

Councils, patwaris) actually apply it — often where women fall into gaps. Conflating these three layers is the single biggest source of bad legal-info products in this space. Example: "can I get khula?" needs all three — Islam permits it; the 1939 Act doesn't even use the word "khula" (developed via case law); in practice, courts now require informed consent rather than automatic conversion of a cruelty case into khula (2026 Supreme Court ruling). 

2. **answer.** Most Pakistani Muslims are Hanafi Sunni, but a 

meaningful Shia (mostly Ithna Ashari) minority exists with structurally different inheritance and family-law rules. Default to Hanafi with a visible toggle/note for Shia users — don't silently pick one. 

3. **Distinguish federal law from provincial amendments.** After the 18th Amendment (2010), family law became provincial. Punjab, Sindh, KP, and Balochistan have each amended base statutes (e.g., MFLO 1961) differently (Punjab's 2015 Amendment Act, Sindh's own reforms). The agent should ask the user's province before jurisdiction-specific answers, or clearly caveat that it's giving the federal/Punjab baseline. 

4. **Track live case law, not just statutes.** Some of the most consequential women's-rights rules (e.g., whether dower is automatically forfeited in khula) are currently unsettled — a 2022 Federal Shariat Court ruling struck down the old statutory formula in Family Courts Act 1964 §10, and superior courts have been filling the gap since, including a significant May 2026 Supreme Court ruling. Build a process to re-check case law quarterly. 

5. **Cite the actual section number every time** government sources (pakistancode.gov.pk, provincial law departments, Federal Shariat Court, Supreme Court judgments) over law-firm blogs for black-letter law. Use law-firm/news sources for practice details and recent case-law summaries, marked as secondary. 

6. 

(if serving Shia users) Shia scholars review the fiqh framing. Not optional for a product shaping real decisions about money, marriage, children.

Consider: Urdu/Roman Urdu output, offline/low-data mode, clear repeated privacy statements, an easy non-alarming exit. Always end sensitive answers (divorce, custody, abuse-adjacent topics) with a pointer to real human help — legal aid or a woman-focused helpline.

topics.legal_basis:
Faraid ("the obligatory shares") derives primarily from **Surah An-Nisa (4), verses 11, 12, and 176** , which fix exact fractional shares for specific relatives ("Quranic heirs"/"sharers") before anyone else inherits. 

- **Quran 4:11** (children & parents): son's share = 2× daughter's share; 2+ daughters with no son jointly take 2/3; a single daughter with no son takes 1/2; each parent takes 1/6 if deceased left children; if no children and only parents inherit, mother takes 1/3 (1/6 if there are siblings) — all after bequests/debts.¹ 

- **Quran 4:12** (spouses): husband inherits 1/2 (no children) or 1/4 (with children); wife/wives collectively inherit 1/4 (no children) or 1/8 (with children) — after bequests/debts.² 

- **Quran 4:176** (siblings, kalalah case — no children/parents) sets siblings' shares.³ 

⁴ 

1. **Sharers (ashab al-furud)** wife, daughter, father, mother, and others (siblings, grandparents) depending on survivors. 

2. **Residuaries (asabah)** — mostly male agnatic relatives (sons, then further male-line relatives) splitting the remainder in fixed priority order. A son always inherits as residuary alongside daughters (daughters are sharers, son absorbs residue — this is how the "male gets 2x female" rule in 4:11 plays out). 

3. **Distant kindred (zawil arham)** — remote relatives (e.g., daughter's children, sister's children), inheriting only if no sharers/ residuaries exist. If no one in any tier survives, the estate escheats to the state. 

_Worked example: man dies leaving a widow and two sons, no other sharers — widow takes 1/8 (he had children); the two sons split the remaining 7/8 equally as residuaries._ ⁵ 

#### **numerically:** 

- Only **two classes** of heirs — sharers and residuaries — no separate "distant kindred" category (folded into class-based system).⁶ 

- Heirs divided into classes by blood/marriage proximity (parents & children; grandparents & siblings; uncles/aunts); a nearer class **fully excludes** a more remote one — unlike Sunni law where sharers and residuaries inherit simultaneously.⁷ 

- Distribution generally follows **per-stirpes** (by branch) logic in several situations, versus the Sunni per-capita approach — can change how much a specific grandchild or sibling's descendant receives.⁸ 

- Shia law allows **radd** (return of leftover residue to sharers, excluding spouses) more broadly, and does not apply the Sunni **aul** doctrine (proportional reduction when shares exceed the whole) the same way.⁹ 

**Product implication:** Cannot build one calculator and relabel it "Shia mode" by changing numbers — needs a separately validated calculation path, ideally reviewed by someone versed in Ithna Ashari fiqh (e.g., Lucy Carroll's comparative academic work is a strong starting citation, not a blog).¹⁰

topics.legal_basis:
- **West Pakistan Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1962** — confirms that for Muslims, "intestate succession, special 

- property of females… marriage, dissolution of marriage… maintenance, dower, guardianship, gifts, trusts and trust properties, and wakfs" are governed by Muslim Personal Law rather than regional custom.¹¹ Deliberate correction: previously many Punjabi/tribal customary rules excluded women from land inheritance entirely. **Section 3** specifically terminates limited/life estates Muslim women held under customary law, replacing them with full ownership under actual Shariat rules.¹² 

- **MFLO 1961, Section 4 — orphaned grandchildren:** modification to classical Hanafi doctrine — if a son/daughter of the deceased predeceased them, that dead child's own children step into their parent's place and inherit per stirpes.¹³ Under strict classical Hanafi law, such grandchildren could be excluded entirely if an uncle/aunt is alive. **This provision has been actively contested** : the Federal Shariat Court has been asked whether Section 4 is compatible with Islamic injunctions, and appeals on this question have been pending before superior courts.¹⁴ **Do not present Section 4 as settled.** 

- **Non-Muslims:** The **Succession Act, 1925** governs substantive inheritance for Christians, Hindus, Parsis, and other non-Muslim Pakistanis, and also supplies general succession-certificate procedure (Sections 370–390) used across communities.¹⁵

topics.title_en: 3.3 Enforcement: Prevention of Anti-Women Practices Act, 2011**
topics.legal_basis:
Arguably the single most important practical law for this space — the core problem is usually not that the law denies women inheritance (Islamic and statutory law both affirm it) but that families pressure, deceive, or forge documents to prevent women from claiming it. 

Amendments to the Pakistan Penal Code: 

- **Section 498-A** inheritance by deceitful/illegal means; punishable by **5–10 years'** 

#### .¹⁶ 

- **Section 498-B** — criminalizes forced marriage (3–10 years plus fine).¹⁷ 

- **Section 498-C** — criminalizes "marriage to the Quran" (coercing a woman to swear on the Quran never to marry, to block her inheritance claim), and targets vani/swara (compensation marriages settling feuds/disputes).¹⁸ 

Independent research reports the Act remains **weakly enforced and not well known** , with ambiguous statutory language and low reporting rates due to family/social pressure.¹⁹ The agent should affirm the law exists and is on women's side, while being honest that enforcement is inconsistent.

topics.title_en: 3.4 How a Woman Actually Claims Her Share — Step by Step**
topics.legal_basis:
1. — from Union Council / NADRA.²⁰ 

2. from NADRA, listing all legal heirs. 

3. **For movable assets** (bank accounts, shares, pensions): a **Succession Certificate** , obtainable either (a) from a Civil Court under Succession Act 1925 §§370–390, or (b) since 2021, via NADRA's Succession Certificate/Letters of Administration system (generally faster).²¹ 

4. **For immovable property** (land, house): apply to the local revenue officer (patwari) for a mutation of ownership ( _intiqal_ ) using the FRC and death certificate; a notice period allows objections before finalization. Disputes go to a partition suit in District Court (or Family Court for some categories).²² 

5. **If excluded by fraud/forgery/coercion:** pursue civil remedies (challenging the succession certificate/mutation in court) and/or a criminal complaint under PPC §498-A. 

A woman does **not** need her brothers' or father's permission to claim her share, and cannot lawfully be made to "sign away" her inheritance under family pressure — such a waiver is exactly what §498-A criminalizes. Courts have held that even a release deed signed during the father's lifetime does not bind a daughter, who can still claim her share after his 

death, absent narrow circumstances like estoppel from a fully executed and benefited-from family settlement.²³

topics.legal_basis:
- **Registration (MFLO s.5):** Every Muslim marriage must be registered with a licensed Nikah Registrar; solemnizing without registration reporting incurs fine/imprisonment. topics.legal_basis: Four broad legal routes to end a Muslim marriage in Pakistan, with differing financial consequences.

qa.question: Divorce**
qa.answer: Four broad legal routes to end a Muslim marriage in Pakistan, with differing financial consequences.

topics.legal_basis:
Governed by **MFLO Section 7** . A husband pronouncing talaq (any form) must give written notice to the Union Council Chairman, with a copy to the wife. Talaq does **not** take legal effect for **90 days** from the Chairman's receipt of notice (or until end of pregnancy, if later) — during 

which the Chairman must form an Arbitration Council to attempt reconciliation. Pronouncing talaq without this notice is an offence (up to 1 year imprisonment and/or fine) — but courts have held the talaq can still be religiously/legally effective even without notice, a real practical gap: an unregistered talaq is hard to prove or disprove later.²⁷

topics.title_en: 5.3 Judicial Divorce Sought by the Wife — Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939**
topics.legal_basis:
Lists the grounds on which a wife can go to Family Court and get judicial dissolution regardless of husband's agreement. **Section 2 grounds:**²⁹ 

1. Husband's whereabouts unknown for 4 years. 

2. Husband neglected/failed to provide maintenance for 2 years. 

3. Husband took an additional wife in violation of MFLO's polygamypermission rule. 

4. Husband sentenced to imprisonment of 7+ years. 

5. Husband failed, without reasonable cause, to perform marital obligations for 3 years. 

6. Husband impotent at time of marriage and remains so. 

7. Husband insane for 2 years, or has leprosy, or a virulent venereal disease. 

- repudiates the marriage before turning 18, if unconsummated. 

9. **Cruelty** even without physical violence; associating with women of ill repute or an infamous life; forcing her into an immoral life; disposing of her property or obstructing her legal rights over it; obstructing her religious practice; in polygamous marriages, 

inequitable treatment per the Quran. 

10. Any other ground recognized as valid under Muslim Law — the "catch-all" courts have used to expand recognized grounds (including, functionally, khula itself). 

**Section 4:** A Muslim woman's conversion away from Islam does **not** by itself dissolve her marriage — she must seek dissolution on one of the above grounds. **Section 5:** using this Act does not affect her right to dower — a separate, independently enforceable right.³⁰

**Section 4:** A Muslim woman's conversion away from Islam does **not** by itself dissolve her marriage — she must seek dissolution on one of the above grounds. **Section 5:** using this Act does not affect her right to dower — a separate, independently enforceable right.³⁰

topics.title_en: 5.4 Khula — the Wife's Right to Release Herself, and What It Costs Her**
topics.legal_basis:
The word "khula" doesn't appear in the 1939 Act's text — it developed through case law reading Islamic khula doctrine into the "any other ground" clause. In practice, courts treat khula as the wife's near-absolute right: she need not prove fault or cruelty — generally enough that she states she cannot continue living within the limits prescribed by God (marriage broken down from her side); courts are bound to grant it.³¹ Husband's consent is not required.³² 

because khula is treated as release in exchange for consideration, courts have traditionally required her to **return the dower** already received (or forgo dower still owed) — the biggest thing women lose compared to dissolution on a proven ground (e.g., cruelty/ non-maintenance), where dower is not automatically forfeited.³³ ³⁴ 

#### **This area is live/unsettled, not settled — recent developments:** 

- **2022:** The Federal Shariat Court struck down subsections (5) and (6) of Family Courts Act 1964 §10, which had given family courts a fixed formula for dower on khula. This created a legal gap being filled case by case since.³⁵ 

- **2026 (Lahore High Court):** Ruled that a wife's dower right remains protected where the marriage was dissolved due to husband's cruelty/misconduct — even if the decree is formally labelled "khula." The court distinguished "khula simpliciter" (pure personal aversion, forfeiture logic still applies) from dissolution caused by husband's fault ("nashuz"), and called on the Punjab 

legislature to enact a clear replacement rule.³⁶ 

- **May 2026 (Supreme Court):** A three-member bench (Chief Justice Yahya Afridi; judgment authored by Justice Shahid Bilal Hassan) held that a family court **cannot automatically convert a cruelty case into a khula case without the wife's clear, informed, and voluntary consent** — because doing so can silently cost her financial rights (especially dower) she'd keep if her cruelty claim succeeded. Where cruelty isn't fully proven but the marriage has genuinely broken down, the wife must still be given the choice to proceed via khula rather than forced to keep litigating fault. The Court set a lower **"preponderance of probability"** evidentiary standard for domestic disputes (rejecting any requirement for eyewitnesses or FIRs), and adopted a broad cruelty definition including sustained mental/emotional abuse, not only physical violence.³⁷ 

**Bottom line for end users:** As of the May 2026 ruling, a woman does not have to choose between "proving cruelty" and "getting khula quickly" as a forced trade-off — courts must explain this choice and get her informed consent before treating her case as khula, because khula can cost her the dower she might otherwise keep. Flag this prominently.

**What it is:** An obligatory payment/property the husband owes the wife as a term of the marriage contract itself — not a gift, not conditional on the marriage lasting, not something the family "keeps." Grounded in **Quran 4:4** ("give the women their due compensation"), recorded in the nikahnama.³⁹ Typically split into: 

- **Prompt dower (mu'ajjal)** — payable immediately/on demand. 

- **Deferred dower (mu'wajjal)** — payable on a triggering event, usually divorce or the husband's death.⁴⁰ 

**When owed, and to whom:** The Supreme Court has explicitly ruled that mehr must be paid **whenever the wife demands it** — not only owed upon divorce. If no timing was specified, she can demand it at any point during the marriage; the debt is enforceable directly against the husband.⁴ **MFLO** ¹ If mode/timing isn't specified in the nikahnama, **Section 10** presumes the entire amount is payable on demand.⁴² 

**Does she lose it if she leaves the marriage?** Genuinely factdependent as of mid-2026: 

- If dissolution is granted on a **proven statutory ground** under the DMMA (non-maintenance, cruelty, unauthorized second marriage) — courts have treated dower as **protected** , even where the decree paperwork says "khula."⁴³ 

- If she seeks release for her **own reasons, unrelated to husband's fault** ("khula simpliciter") — courts have traditionally directed her to return prompt dower already paid (or an agreed/ admitted portion) and treated unpaid deferred dower as forfeited — though not automatic anymore post-2022/2026; fact- and judge-dependent.⁴⁴ 

- If husband takes a **second wife without following MFLO permission procedure** , this is treated as his fault — a wife divorcing over this generally is not required to return dower; at least one reported Supreme Court case restored her full dower.⁴⁵ 

**Procedure:** Dower is recovered via a suit in Family Court under the Family Courts Act, 1964, regardless of how the marriage ended (talaq, khula, or judicial dissolution), so long as it hasn't already been paid or formally waived.⁴⁶

topics.legal_basis:
**During marriage:** A husband is legally obligated to maintain his wife (food, clothing, shelter, medical needs) regardless of her own income; 

her working does not reduce/excuse this obligation. If he fails, she can **MFLO Section 9** Arbitration seek a maintenance certificate via the Council process, and/or sue directly in Family Court. Generally survives even if she lives separately, provided she has a valid reason (cruelty, his failure to provide a home) — a wife found "disobedient" ( _nashiza_ ) without valid cause can lose this claim, a genuinely contested and gendered doctrine to present carefully.⁴⁷ ⁴⁸ 

**During iddat** (post-divorce waiting period): husband remains obligated to maintain her through iddat — **three menstrual cycles/three months** after divorce, or until childbirth if pregnant (Quran 65:4), or **four months and ten days** if a widow.⁴⁹ Pakistani case law: PLD 1981 Karachi 240 confirms maintenance is obligatory during iddat but not automatically beyond it "unless agreed"; PLD 2003 Lahore 15 confirmed a pregnant divorced wife's maintenance continues until childbirth regardless of iddat's normal length.⁵⁰ _(Note: these case citations are reported via secondary sources — verify against original PLD law reports before publishing to end users.)_ 

**After iddat:** A divorced wife is generally **not entitled to further maintenance for herself** once iddat ends, unless she has a separate agreement/contractual right — differs from some other Muslim-majority jurisdictions and broader statutory frameworks (e.g., India's CrPC) that extend it further; Pakistan's system does not currently do so as a matter of course.⁵¹ 

**Children's maintenance** is separate and does **not** end with the marriage. A father remains obligated to maintain his children until adulthood/financial independence, regardless of custody arrangements — even if the mother has custody (hizanat), the father must still pay child maintenance directly.⁵²

topics.legal_basis:
- **Hizanat (custody):** day-to-day physical care and upbringing. 

- **Wilayat (guardianship):** for the child. 

Governed by the **Guardians and Wards Act, 1890** ; **Section 17** sets the overriding legal test: **the welfare of the minor** — not either parent's "right" — is paramount.⁵³ Islamic hizanat doctrine supplies the starting presumption, tested against actual child welfare: 

- **Mother's presumptive custody:** sons until ~age 7; daughters until puberty (Hanafi position).⁵⁴ 

- This presumption is **rebuttable** — the other parent can contest with evidence it wouldn't serve the child's welfare; courts do depart from it when warranted.⁵⁵ 

- court, she may lose the presumption.⁵⁶ 

- After the presumptive custody period ends, the father (as natural guardian) generally becomes entitled to physical custody too, again subject to welfare review — not automatic.⁵⁷ 

- **Custody is legally independent of how the marriage ended.** A mother who obtains khula does not lose custody rights by virtue of that alone; a father who pronounces talaq does not automatically gain custody.⁵⁸ 

- **Interim custody** can be granted under **Section 12** while a full custody case (a full trial, not a quick hearing) is pending; the parent without interim custody generally retains visitation rights.⁵⁹ 

- If both parents are unavailable, custody priority typically passes to other relatives (e.g., maternal/paternal grandmother), in an order recognized by fiqh and applied by courts.⁶⁰ 

**Procedure:** File a petition under the Guardians and Wards Act before the Guardian/Family Court where the child resides; other parent is served notice and can respond; courts often attempt reconciliation first; interim custody/visitation can be set while pending; final order turns on welfare factors (stability, education, child's own wishes at sufficient age, character of each parent, etc.); appeal lies to the High Court.⁶¹

topics.title_en: 9. Q&A Bank (Draft — Adapt for the Agent)**
topics.legal_basis:
_Each answer is deliberately short and points to the fuller sourced section above. Treat as drafts for counsel review, not final user-facing copy._ 

**Q: Can my father or brothers legally stop me from inheriting?** No. Under Islamic law and the West Pakistan Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1962, your inheritance share is a legal right, not something the family grants. Deliberately depriving you of it by deceit, pressure, or forged documents is a specific criminal offence under PPC §498-A (5–10 years' imprisonment and/or fine up to Rs. 1 million). (§3.3) 

**Q: Can I be made to sign away my inheritance?** A document signed under family pressure is not automatically binding; courts have held such waivers do not bar you from later claiming your actual share, except in narrow circumstances (e.g., a fully executed family settlement you knowingly benefited from). (§3.4) 

**Q: How much do I actually inherit as a daughter?** Depends who else survives (sons, parents, spouse, siblings) and your school of thought. General Hanafi Sunni rule: one daughter alone gets half the estate; two+ daughters together get two-thirds (before residuaries take the rest); if a son is also alive, daughters and sons split 1 female : 2 male shares of what's left after other sharers are paid. Shia calculation differs structurally, not just numerically — flag this and ask the user's sect before calculating. (§3.1) 

**Q: Do I lose my inheritance if I get divorced or remarry?** No — inheritance rights from your parents/family are unrelated to marital status. (Divorce affects rights against your ex-husband's estate specifically; dower is a separate right — see §6.) 

**Q: What do I need to actually collect my share?** Family Registration Certificate from NADRA listing all heirs, then either a succession certificate (movable assets — via NADRA or civil court) or a mutation at the revenue office/patwari (immovable property/land). If contested, a partition suit in court. (§3.4) 

**Q: My husband wants to marry a second wife. Can he, and what are my rights?** Only with prior written permission from an Arbitration Council, which must find it "necessary and just" and consider your consent. If he marries again without permission, the law requires him to pay your full dower immediately, and you may use this as grounds to 

seek dissolution without necessarily losing your dower. (§4, §5.1) 

**Q: Can I get divorced without my husband's agreement?** Yes, two routes: (1) judicial dissolution under the DMMA 1939 if you show one of nine specific grounds (non-maintenance for 2 years, cruelty, unauthorized second marriage, etc.); or (2) khula, which courts treat as close to an absolute right — you generally don't need to prove fault, just that you cannot continue living within the marriage's limits. His consent is not required for either. (§5.3, §5.4) 

**Q: If I get khula, do I lose my Haq Mehr?** Depends on why the marriage is ending. If genuinely your own choice with no fault on his side, courts traditionally direct you to return dower already paid. If the real cause is his cruelty, non-maintenance, or misconduct, courts (especially since the May 2026 Supreme Court ruling) are supposed to keep that distinct from ordinary khula and protect your dower — even if the paperwork says "khula." This area is actively evolving as of 2026; get case-specific advice. (§5.4, §6) 

**Q: Can I demand my mehr any time, or only at divorce?** You can demand it any time during the marriage if no specific timing was agreed in the nikahnama — the Supreme Court has confirmed mehr must be paid whenever the wife demands it, not only upon divorce. (§6) 

**Q: Is my husband required to support me if he's not divorcing me but we're separated?** Generally yes, if you have a valid reason for living separately (cruelty, his failure to provide housing) — you can file a maintenance case in Family Court even without seeking divorce. (§7) 

**Q: Does my husband have to support me after divorce?** Only through your iddat period (~3 months, or until childbirth if pregnant) — unless you have a separate agreement. Support for your children continues regardless, until they're grown, and is unaffected by custody. (§7) 

##### 

**divorce?** No — custody is legally independent of how/why the marriage ended. Under the Hanafi presumption applied by Pakistani courts, mothers generally keep custody of sons until ~age 7 and daughters until puberty, always subject to the court's assessment of the child's actual welfare. (§8) 

**Q: What if my husband tries to take the children away from me?** He would need to go through the Guardian/Family Court under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 — he cannot simply take them; you can seek interim custody and, if warranted, a protective order while the matter is decided. (§8) 

**Q: I think I'm being forced into a marriage / my family wants me to marry to settle a dispute (vani/swara).** This is a specific criminal offence under PPC §498-B (forced marriage) and, for dispute-settlement marriages like vani/swara, also §498-C. (§3.3) — **This should also trigger a safety/escalation response, not just a legal-information answer** (see §1, point 8).

topics.title_en: 11. Explicit Gaps and Next Research Steps**
topics.legal_basis:
- **Provincial variation** beyond Punjab is only lightly covered — Sindh, KP, Balochistan, GB, and AJK may each have their own MFLO/Family Courts Act amendments. Needs a dedicated pass per province. 

- **Domestic violence law** (e.g., provincial Domestic Violence Acts) is referenced only tangentially through the 2026 SC cruelty ruling — deserves its own dedicated research document, especially given the safety-escalation point in §1. 

- **Christian, Hindu, and Parsi personal law** in Pakistan (marriage, divorce, inheritance under the Succession Act 1925 and community-specific statutes like the Divorce Act 1869 for Christians) is out of scope here but matters if the user base isn't 

exclusively Muslim. 

- **Actual PLD/SCMR law-report citations** referenced via secondary sources (e.g., PLD 1981 Karachi 240) should be pulled and verified from original law reports before publishing to end users. 

- A §3.1) is a real gap if the product intends to serve Shia users with numeric answers. 

- A **live-monitoring process** for Federal Shariat Court and Supreme Court family-law rulings is needed — this field visibly moved in 2022, 2023, and again in May and July 2026 alone.

qa.answer:
- **Provincial variation** beyond Punjab is only lightly covered — Sindh, KP, Balochistan, GB, and AJK may each have their own MFLO/Family Courts Act amendments. Needs a dedicated pass per province.

- **Christian, Hindu, and Parsi personal law** in Pakistan (marriage, divorce, inheritance under the Succession Act 1925 and community-specific statutes like the Divorce Act 1869 for Christians) is out of scope here but matters if the user base isn't
